candidate_relations.reason: Small unilateral renal stones and normal renal function do not establish primary hyperoxaluria, which would require a systemic oxalate phenotype.
Dysmorphic erythrocytes can suggest glomerular bleeding, but no biopsy or persistent proteinuric glomerular findings establish thin basement membrane nephropathy.
Posterior nutcracker phenomenon describes the compression anatomy alone, whereas six years of recurrent hematuria makes the reference a symptomatic syndrome.
The record contains no proteinuria, renal impairment, or biopsy evidence supporting IgA nephropathy despite dysmorphic red cells.
Left renal vein compression is the vascular basis of nutcracker syndrome, but the label omits the posterior course and symptomatic hematuria.
Normal renal function and absence of proteinuria or nephritic serologies leave glomerulonephritis unsupported as the source of hematuria.
No urinary calcium measurement or recurrent calcium-stone history is provided to diagnose hypercalciuria.
Recurrent objective hematuria over six years requires an explanation and is incompatible with the candidate stating no diagnosis.
Hypertension was diagnosed two years earlier and treated with irbesartan, but it does not explain the posterior left renal vein compression syndrome.
There is no purpura, abdominal vasculitic syndrome, proteinuria, or renal biopsy evidence for Henoch-Schönlein purpura nephritis.
No systemic lupus features, serology, complement abnormality, or proteinuric renal disease is reported.
Ultrasound showed sand-like stones but no collecting-duct ectasia or nephrocalcinosis characteristic of medullary sponge kidney.
Neither family history nor renal biopsy evidence supports thin basement membrane disease in this vascular-compression case.
Multiple small calculi were described within the left kidney, not diffuse medullary calcium deposition diagnostic of nephrocalcinosis.
The reference requires posterior compression, whereas anterior nutcracker syndrome involves the conventional vein compressed between the aorta and superior mesenteric artery.
Fatty liver was an incidental ultrasound finding and has no mechanistic link to the recurrent hematuria.
The sand-like stones were present, but the record explicitly treats them as unlikely to account for the longstanding bleeding.
The candidate exactly identifies posterior nutcracker syndrome, the vascular diagnosis used to explain the recurrent painless hematuria.
No hearing, ocular, family-history, or progressive renal-function abnormalities suggest Alport syndrome.
Ultrasound confirmed small left renal stones, but their incidental nature and painless intermittent course do not replace the vascular diagnosis.
